extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and parties participating in PTAB inter partes review proceedings (petitioners, patent owners, litigators, expert witnesses)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria used by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board to evaluate patentability in an inter partes review: burden of proof, anticipation (§102), obviousness (§103) (Graham/KSR), claim construction, enablement, level of ordinary skill, and how to weigh prior art and evidence (expert testimony, examples, priority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of persuasion in IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: In an IPR, the petitioner has the burden from the onset to show with particularity why the patent it challenges is unpatentable; this burden of persuasion never shifts to Patent Owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Harmonic Inc. v. Avid Tech. and 35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3). A petition must identify with particularity the evidence supporting each ground for each claim. The Board applies the preponderance of the evidence standard in the Final Written Decision (35 U.S.C. § 318(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation under 35 U.S.C. §102
rubrics_metrics.description: A single prior art reference must expressly or inherently disclose each claim limitation; the reference must describe the claimed invention with sufficient precision and detail to establish that the subject matter existed in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Finisar Corp. v. DirecTV Grp., Verve, LLC v. Crane Cams, Inc. and In re Preda. Inherency for anticipation requires that the missing descriptive material be 'necessarily present,' not merely probable. Consider not only explicit teachings but the inferences a POSITA would reasonably draw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency standard (for anticipation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A finding of inherency requires that the missing descriptive material is 'necessarily present' in the prior art reference, not merely probably or possibly present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Trindec Indus. v. Top-USA Corp. and In re Robertson: inherency is a strict test. However, it is proper to consider reasonable inferences a person of ordinary skill would draw from the reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness under 35 U.S.C. §103 (Graham/KSR framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the Graham factual inquiries (scope/content of prior art; differences between the prior art and claims; level of ordinary skill; objective evidence) and KSR's expansive/flexible approach to obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR explains that combining old elements that perform their known functions in a predictable way can be obvious. A petitioner must show a POSITA would have been motivated to combine references and would have had a reasonable expectation of success. A precise teaching directed to the claimed subject matter is not necessary; any known need or problem can provide motivation to combine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine and reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish obviousness, show (1) a motivation that would have led a POSITA to combine the prior art teachings and (2) a reasonable expectation of success in doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites KSR and In re Magnum Oil Tools. Expectation of success need only be reasonable, not absolute; some unpredictability does not defeat obviousness. Evidence such as prior art demonstrating similar constructs, common usage in the field, or authoritative expert testimony can support motivation and reasonable expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the level of skill by considering the type of problems in the art, prior art solutions, rapidity of innovation, sophistication of the technology, and educational level of active workers; POSITA may be a team with complementary skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board accepted defining the POSITA as having the skills of a research team (e.g., molecular biology/virology researchers together with protein engineering experts). Evidence and expert testimony (declarations) are used to define the POSITA's knowledge and capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are construed under the same standard used in civil actions (35 U.S.C. § 282(b)); claim words are given their ordinary and customary meaning to a POSITA at the time of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary sources are intrinsic evidence: the claim language, the written description, and the prosecution history. Only terms in controversy need be construed and only to the extent necessary to resolve the dispute (citing Phillips and Nidec Motor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement / sufficiency of prior art disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference must provide enough disclosure (precision, detail, and enablement) to teach or enable practice of the claimed invention for it to anticipate or to be used in an obviousness combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Owner may argue a reference is non-enabling. The Board examines the reference's examples, claimed preferred embodiments, and whether a POSITA could practice the claimed invention without undue experimentation. Lack of enabling disclosure can defeat anticipation or reduce weight of a reference in an obviousness analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight to be given to preferred embodiments and examples in prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing a reference, the Board considers explicit disclosures, preferred embodiments, individual claims, and worked examples as stronger evidence of what the reference teaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision stresses that preferred embodiments and specifically-claimed variants (e.g., Stafford's explicit R338L and R338A recitations) materially affect whether a reference teaches a limitation. The Board will treat a reference 'for all that it teaches' and will not ignore adjacent or secondary statements (e.g., gene therapy discussion next to vector disclosure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of objective indicia (secondary considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence of non-obviousness (commercial success, long-felt need, copying, unexpected results) must be considered in the obviousness inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors may be given limited or substantial weight depending on the record. The Board will weigh them alongside the Graham factors and may give them little weight if not persuasively supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation and weighing of expert testimony and other evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert declarations, depositions, and other documentary evidence are weighed in light of the whole record to determine issues like enablement, POSITA knowledge, motivation to combine, and expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board credits or discounts expert opinions based on their support in the record, consistency with other evidence, and the expert's reasoning. Testimony that fills gaps with unsupported speculation is given little weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirements and jurisdictional considerations in IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural rules govern petitions and decisions: petitions must identify evidence with particularity (35 U.S.C. §312(a)(3)); the Board has jurisdiction under 35 U.S.C. §6; Final Written Decisions are issued under 35 U.S.C. §318(a); parties seeking judicial review must follow notice/service rules (37 C.F.R. § 90.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board may institute IPR based on a reasonable likelihood of success; the decision stage requires preponderance of the evidence. Patent Owner is reminded of obligations (e.g., notifying Board of reissue or reexamination filings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority/chain-of-priority and its effect on prior art dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing the correct effective filing/priority date is necessary to determine which prior art is available against the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board considers the chain of continuation and priority claims (e.g., PCT and foreign filings) and accepts parties' unopposed assumptions where appropriate. The assumed priority date affects whether references are pre- or post-date for anticipation/obviousness analysis.
